To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) alternative secondary forests in the Central Amazon initiated from different land‐use types exhibit divergent species compositions that persist through two decades of succession; (ii) the divergent species compositions result from the replacement of the dominant pioneer species by other species that are characteristic of each pathway; and (iii) the divergent pathways result from the persistence of land‐use effects that influence species composition and successional trajectories.
Following disturbance, two alternative successional pathways in Central Amazonia, clear‐cut and pastures, diverged through time, with the former dominated by Cecropias and the latter by Vismia.
the species composition of abandoned pasture and clear‐cut sites in central Amazonia diverged over two decades of succession.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamics and mechanisms of species assemblages in secondary forests of Central Amazonia.
the effects of prior land use on the structure and function of tropical forest ecosystems, and with the mechanisms that determine the course of forest succession.
understanding how alternative successional pathways develop and converge in Central Amazonian secondary forests.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two pathways are diverging.
the two pathways diverge through time, and this is due to the differential dominance and replacement of the pioneer species.
the two alternative successions in the Central Amazon are diverging, and the divergence is due to the differential effects of prior land use.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
land‐use history has a long‐lasting effect on the composition of species assemblages.
the initial species composition of secondary forests, as well as the species composition of the climax forest, are determined by the prior land use.

, in the absence of further disturbance, the two pathways converge toward a similar climax community, but that convergence is delayed and the two pathways diverge for a time, with the rate of convergence being greater for the pasture pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of prior land use on species composition persists well beyond the initial floristic composition, even when the initial dominant species have been lost.
even after 20 years of succession, alternative successional trajectories can be distinguished by their species composition.
the initial composition of species in secondary forests is strongly affected by land use, and that this initial effect persists for many years.
